subject: Coffee & Tea
title: How to Store Aged Tea
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on How to Store Aged Tea.

hook.text: Pu-erh aging isn't passive. Storage conditions determine whether a cake matures beautifully or turns to mold.

buildup.text: Ideal storage needs controlled humidity (60–70%), moderate temperature, darkness, and clean air circulation.

discovery.text: Hong Kong's humid climate produces faster, deeper aging. Dry Kunming storage yields slower, brighter results.

twist.text: Mold and off-flavors develop if humidity exceeds 85%. One bad season can ruin decades of patient aging.

climax.text: Serious collectors maintain dedicated humidity-controlled rooms just for their tea collections.

punchline.text: Great pu-erh needs a patient owner and a well-kept room.

quiz.question: What is the ideal humidity range for aging pu-erh?

details.summary: Proper tea storage protects against moisture, light, heat, and odors that degrade quality. Teas intended for aging, like pu-erh and some oolongs, need controlled humidity and airflow. Green and white teas kept sealed in cool, dark conditions retain freshness for months to years.
details.whyItMatters: Bad storage ruins good tea faster than anything else. Understanding storage is as important as understanding brewing for getting the most from your tea.
takeaways: Keep tea away from moisture, light, heat, and strong odors
Aging teas need humidity and airflow; fresh teas need sealed storage
Pu-erh and roasted oolongs can improve with proper aging

faq.question: Can green tea go bad if stored poorly?
faq.answer: Green tea does not become unsafe but rapidly loses freshness. Exposure to heat, light, or oxygen oxidizes the leaves, turning bright flavors flat and stale within months. Refrigerating sealed green tea extends freshness significantly. Japanese teas are especially sensitive.

faq.question: What is the ideal humidity for aging pu-erh?
faq.answer: About 60 to 75 percent relative humidity promotes the microbial activity needed for aging without encouraging mold. Too dry and the tea ages too slowly. Too humid and mold develops. Traditional storage in Guangdong and Hong Kong provides naturally suitable conditions.
